title: Why Winter Makes Your Body Act Strange (Cold, Cough, Joint Pain Explained)
description: Why do your hands go cold, your nose run and your joints ache in winter? Why do we catch colds more often? Step by step, this video shows how your body protects its core, why viruses spread more in winter, and simple ways to stay comfortable. General information, not medical advice.
comment: What is the first thing that goes cold on you in winter? Tell me below!

scenes.text: Why do your hands and feet go icy in winter, your nose run, your joints ache, and why do you catch a cold more often? It feels like your body is fighting the weather. Today we go inside your body to see what really happens when it gets cold.

Your body is like a heater that must stay near thirty seven degrees. Deep inside, your organs work best at that exact temperature. So the moment the air around you turns cold, your brain gets an alarm: protect the core at any cost.

Skin has tiny temperature sensors. When they feel cold, they send a signal to the brain's thermostat, called the hypothalamus. It decides in a fraction of a second what to do. And its first move is to save heat, not to keep your fingers warm.

First trick: blood vessels near your skin become narrow. Less warm blood reaches your hands, feet and nose, so they lose heat slowly. That is why they turn cold, pale or even blue. Your body is sacrificing the edges to protect the middle.

Ever noticed that cold fingers hurt when they warm up? As warm blood rushes back into the narrowed vessels, your nerves wake up all at once and fire together. You feel burning and pins and needles. It is uncomfortable, but it is a sign that blood flow is returning.

Second trick: goosebumps. Each tiny hair has a tiny muscle. In the cold, it pulls the hair upright. Furry animals trap a warm layer of air this way. Humans lost most of their fur, so we just get bumps, a leftover from our past.

Third trick: shivering. Your muscles contract rapidly, again and again, and burning energy makes heat. A strong shiver can make several times more heat than resting. That is why you feel hungry and tired after a cold day.

There is also a quiet heater inside you: brown fat. Normal fat stores energy. Brown fat burns it directly to make heat. Babies have lots of it, and adults keep a little near the neck and shoulders. Cold exposure can wake it up.

Here is a funny one: why do you need the toilet more in winter? When blood vessels narrow, more blood stays in your core. Your kidneys notice the extra blood, filter more of it, and make more urine. Scientists call this cold diuresis. You also drink less in winter, so staying hydrated matters.

So why do you get cold, cough and flu more often in winter? Many people think the cold air itself makes you sick. But the cold only helps the real culprits: viruses. They are always around, and winter gives them three advantages.

Advantage one: in the cold, the lining of your nose becomes drier and the tiny hairs that sweep germs away move more slowly. Your first defence weakens. Cold, dry air also lets some viruses survive longer in the air and on surfaces.

Advantage two: we stay indoors with the windows closed. Many people share the same air, so one sneeze reaches everyone. Advantage three: less sunlight means less vitamin D, which your immune cells use. Together, these give viruses an easy win.

Winter also makes you sleepy and a little low. Short days mean less sunlight reaching your eyes. Your brain makes more melatonin, the sleep hormone, and less serotonin, a mood chemical. That is why getting out of bed feels harder, and why a little morning sunlight helps so much.

Now the sore joints. Doctors are still studying this, but one idea is that when air pressure drops before cold weather, the tissues around joints swell slightly and press on nerves. Cold also makes muscles stiffer and thicker joint fluid moves less smoothly.

Then the runny nose. Your nose warms and humidifies the air you breathe. In cold air, the warm moist breath hits the cold nose lining, and water condenses, just like drops on a cold glass. That is why your nose drips when you walk outside.

And the dry, cracked lips and skin? Winter air holds very little water, so it pulls moisture out of your skin. The skin's protective oily layer cracks. Hot showers make it worse because they wash away the natural oils.

If the cold goes too far, body parts can freeze. In frostbite, skin and tissue lose blood flow for so long that ice crystals form and damage the cells. Fingers, toes, ears and nose suffer first. Warm the area gently, never rub it, and see a doctor.

So how do you stay comfortable? Wear layers, because trapped air between layers is a wonderful insulator. Cover your head, neck, hands and feet, where your body loses the most heat. Wool and cotton blends keep you warm even when slightly damp.

Drink warm fluids and eat regular meals, since your body burns extra energy to stay warm. Keep moving a little, because muscles make heat. Wash your hands often, and open windows for a few minutes daily so that fresh air can carry viruses out.

One myth to drop: alcohol does not warm you. It widens blood vessels near the skin, so you feel warm for a moment, but you actually lose more heat. And a woollen sweater does not create heat; it just holds the heat your body already makes.

Know the warning signs. If someone shivers badly, speaks slowly, becomes confused or very sleepy, or their skin turns very pale, that can be a sign of dangerous cold exposure. Move them somewhere warm and get medical help quickly.

So winter is not your body failing. It is your body working very hard: saving heat, shivering, fighting viruses and protecting your core. Now you know the science behind every chill. If you liked this, subscribe, and tell me which topic you want next.
